Question: Is there a gas molecule heavier than water?
Answer: By “heavier”, do you mean having a higher molecular mass than water (> 18.01528 g/mol)? There are plenty of gases that fit that bill. Question: Is it better to do a postdoc at a famous university or with a famous postdoc advisor at a state university?

Question: Are CF2 and CCl2 real chemical compounds?
Answer: To build on Mark B Fischer’s answer, difluorocarbene and dichlorocarbene (CF2 and CCl2) can be generated during reactions, but since their lifetimes are very short, they cannot be isolated and stored. Carbenes are rather reactive, and once formed, will react with other electron donors/acceptors or dimerize/oligomerize with themselves. It’s pretty easy to form difluorocarbene or dichlorocarbene; a common way is to generate the trihalo carbanion (by deprotonation of chloroform or CF3H with KOtBu or similar bases), which then undergoes α-dehalogenation to give the dihalocarbene.

Question: What is the deal if someone graduated with a PhD from a prestigious school, as opposed to an average school?
Answer: Prestigious or well-known schools will give you a massive boost in the job market. Having a name like “Harvard”, “Stanford”, “Princeton”, “MIT”, “Caltech”, or “Berkeley” on your resume/CV will open up so many more doors for you that would otherwise have remained closed if you didn’t attend those schools. Well-known schools will have a lot more companies who will come to recruit graduates, and professors at top institutions are more likely to have connections with companies that will help in landing you that elusive first job after graduation. I did my PhD at a lower-ranked institution, and we had zero companies coming to recruit students from our department. The sad thing is that even though there may be negligible differences between PhD students at various institutions (in terms of domain knowledge, skill, or work ability), a lot of employers will prefer students from the aforementioned prestigious schools, due to brand recognition. It’s the same reason why you would prefer to wear a Hugo Boss suit or buy a Hermes bag rather then get some cheap knockoff.

Question: Do I have to be a genius or have a PhD to be a scientist?
Answer: Absolutely not. Grit, perseverance, hard work, and tenacity are much more important qualities for a scientist than being a “genius”. This doesn’t require being a genius or having a PhD, just having the domain knowledge to know what’s going on. As Louis Pasteur said, “In the fields of observation chance favors only the prepared mind.”

Question: How did Ph.D students become so good at writing?
Answer: Please don’t generalize; I have known a lot of Ph.D. students who were objectively terrible writers. That being said… As others here have mentioned, practice is a big component. I would also imagine that growing up in an English-speaking country and attending English-medium schools would also help a lot. Any writer worth his or her salt will also tell you that reading a lot is extremely important; that’s how you learn about acceptable conventions, idioms, flow, and what works in the domain you’re interested in. Getting timely and constructive feedback from other good writers is also invaluable; this is a critical step in being able to grow as a writer, as it is right there that others will point out the good and bad elements in your writing. Also, keep in mind that a lot of what you read that is written by Ph.D.s (e.g. scientific articles, reviews, books, chapters, etc.) will probably have been edited hundreds of times before publication, so is more likely to be a group rather than solo effort.

Question: Why do you always have to do the same job as past experience on your resume? Why can't someone change their career?
Answer: The answer to your first question is largely due to two factors: In a highly competitive job market, hiring managers will often become extremely risk-averse, because they can afford to be picky and choose the perfect candidate out of the applicant pool. Why should he/she consider someone who has similar but not exact qualifications when there are plenty of others who fit the requirements to a T? Applicant Tracking System (ATS) software is also biased towards choosing applicants who fit all the requirements exactly, since it filters by keywords and similarity. The software is not smart enough to consider applicants who would be able to do the job just fine even if their experience and education is not a 100% match to the requirements. Changing career paths is possible, but it requires someone to take a chance on you and is largely a function of how well you can convince the potential employer to take you on. This is usually easier after you’ve worked for a few years and developed a network and “transferable” skills.

Question: Does the salary for people with Ph.Ds make the time and money invested in the degree worth it?
Answer: Most of the time, no - the salary premium for a PhD over a master’s degree is not that high. If you’re lucky, a PhD may command a 30% salary premium over a master’s degree, and that’s only if the employer values the skills/knowledge you have obtained. In most cases the PhD is not a wise decision as the opportunity cost is extremely high (5+ years of lost earnings/career growth, and early 401K contributions which are the most valuable as they would have had the longest time to compound). Anecdotally, I have 2 friends my age who are millionaires, and both of them do not have PhD’s.
